title: Appeal evidence: Citation concern remained secondary
desc: Distinguishes possible citation-integrity problems from findings about functional incapacity, procedural fairness and the appeal’s underlying merits.

kps.k: The supplied Bandla extracts establish a citation-integrity concern, not a demonstrated AI hallucination or the strike-out described in the source title.
kps.d: The judge flags serious concerns about authorities in maintained appeal grounds and records that the SRA’s solicitors assembled 53 cited cases that exist. However, the judge expressly sets that issue aside for later consideration. The supplied material therefore does not establish that 25 authorities were nonexistent, that the court struck out grounds for abuse of process, or that generative AI produced the citations. Its contribution to the legal-AI debate is qualified: citation concerns, findings of fabrication, procedural sanctions and attribution to AI require separate evidence.

qs.q: As to cases “which exist”, there is in this case a specific and very serious concern about caselaw which the Appellant cited to the court in grounds of appeal which he has maintained.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The SRA’s solicitors have, as I have explained, also prepared a bundle containing the 53 cases cited by the Appellant which exist.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The substantive ruling distinguishes evidence of mental illness from evidence that illness explains a missed appeal deadline.
kps.d: Applying J v K, the judge requires independent support covering the relevant period and a connection between the condition and the delay. A directly relevant medical report is preferable, but indirect evidence can suffice. Illness that substantially causes delay will usually justify an extension, subject to other parties’ interests, especially after lengthy delay. The judge refuses an extension because the evidence does not establish the asserted inability to appeal, rather than because mental illness cannot justify procedural accommodation.

qs.q: Such a conclusion cannot usually be safely reached simply on their say-so and will require independent support of some kind.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Mental ill-health is of many different kinds and degrees…***  ***(3)***  ***If the tribunal finds that the failure to institute the appeal in time was indeed the result (wholly or in substantial part) of the applicants mental ill-health, justice will usually require the grant of an extension.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The central factual dispute concerns continuous functional incapacity, not whether the appellant ever experienced serious illness.
kps.d: The appellant attributes delay from August 2015 to February 2024 to schizophrenia-related inability to understand or communicate, followed by difficulty securing affordable representation. The judge acknowledges evidence of illness and rehabilitation but identifies gaps in timing and severity. Regulatory activity in 2015, travel and employment after rehabilitation, and clinical records of stability in 2022–2023 contradict the claimed continuous incapacity. The judge regards the post-February 2022 evidence as sufficient to defeat that explanation without resolving every earlier period. Practically, an applicant needs evidence linking functional limitations to the relevant delay, not diagnosis or treatment records alone.

qs.q: His position is that this description of an inability to “understand” or “communicate”, due to delusional problems arising from schizophrenia, continued from 1 August 2015 right through to July 2017 and through to February 2024.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But there are also gaps in terms of the severity of the condition and whether it went as far as to deny him the ability to “understand” and “communicate”; even to the point of his “understanding” that he was a solicitor; that there were SDT proceedings and documents; that he could participate and then subsequently – and most relevantly for present purposes – that he could lodge an appeal.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Procedural fairness and the appeal’s underlying merits provide additional grounds for rejecting the appellant’s position.
kps.d: Proceeding on the SRA’s acceptance that PD52D paragraph 3.3A applies, the judge dates the appeal period from the sending of reasons on 22 June 2017 and rejects inconsistent accounts of receipt. The judge also finds no strong procedural-unfairness case: the SDT considered the available mental-health evidence, approached proceeding in absence cautiously and weighed possible prejudice against the public interest. Changing, unsupported insurance-fraud allegations further weaken the merits. The failure to share a late medical letter despite an express direction adds a practical reminder to comply with document-sharing requirements. These findings remain independent of the unresolved citation issue.

qs.q: The answer in the present case is that the SDT’s “statement of reasons” was “sent to the Appellant” on 22 June 2017.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: I am unable to accept that there is anything approaching a strong case, as the Appellant claims, based on any procedural impropriety on the part of the SDT.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The court/regulatory voice represented here supports the cluster’s principal proposition. The judgment separates a serious citation-integrity concern from the grounds actually analysed: it expressly defers the citation issue and instead rests the refusal of an extension on missing evidence connecting mental illness to the prolonged delay, reinforced by weaknesses in procedural-fairness arguments and the underlying merits. This evidentially disciplined approach also supports the synthesis’s warning not to infer nonexistent authorities, generative-AI involvement or citation-related sanctions from concern alone. The main internal qualification is that the court does regard the maintained citations as raising a serious issue; its position is therefore not that citation integrity was irrelevant, but that the supplied extracts do not resolve it and it was secondary to the operative analysis. Because the curated evidence contains only one source in this professional voice, no broader claim about regulators, courts or professional bodies generally—and no source-to-source variation within that group—can be established.

qs.q: Applying the guidance of Underhill LJ from J v K, it is very clear that the sort of evidence needed, covering the relevant periods of time, so as to explain or excuse the failure to institute an appeal, is absent in this case.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: For now, I put that matter entirely to one side.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The sole supplied 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition, though this curated record cannot establish how prevalent that view was among other sources or groups. Its central reasoning is that the citation-integrity issue was serious but expressly deferred, so the extracts do not themselves demonstrate AI-generated hallucinations, 25 nonexistent authorities or a strike-out on that basis. Instead, the operative analysis turns on evidential gaps linking mental illness to the prolonged delay, reinforced by weaknesses concerning procedural fairness and the underlying merits. The main internal variation is therefore one of emphasis rather than disagreement: the source recognizes a material citation concern while keeping it analytically separate from the grounds deciding the extension-of-time issue.

qs.q: Applying the guidance of Underhill LJ from J v K, it is very clear that the sort of evidence needed, covering the relevant periods of time, so as to explain or excuse the failure to institute an appeal, is absent in this case.
